title: Room acoustic preferences of orchestral musicians: a large-scale in-situ study across 24 concert halls
abstract: Concert hall acoustics are usually evaluated from the perspective of the audience, yet performers themselves rely on stage acoustics to hear one another and to shape their playing. We conducted an in-situ study with 312 professional orchestral musicians across 24 European concert halls, combining questionnaire ratings with binaural impulse response measurements taken at each player's seat. Support parameters (ST_early, ST_late) explained only part of the variance in perceived ease of ensemble; a newly derived measure combining early lateral energy with stage riser geometry predicted ratings substantially better. Wind and brass players were markedly more sensitive to late stage energy than strings. The results suggest that stage acoustic design criteria should be instrument-group specific rather than uniform.
venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

title: Sparse Latent Diffusion for Controllable Symbolic Music Generation
abstract: Recent symbolic music generation models produce fluent material but offer limited control over musical attributes that composers actually care about, such as harmonic rhythm, voice leading density, and phrase boundaries. We introduce a latent diffusion model operating on a sparse event representation in which each latent dimension is regularised to align with an interpretable musical attribute. Training on a corpus of 180k MIDI performances, the model supports attribute-wise conditioning at inference time without retraining. In a listening study with 48 trained musicians, our conditional generations were rated as more stylistically coherent than a transformer baseline, and attribute edits were perceived as intended in 81% of trials. We release code and pretrained checkpoints.

title: Musical chills and the reward system: a preregistered replication with 240 participants
abstract: Music-induced chills have been repeatedly linked to dopaminergic reward circuitry, but the underlying studies have typically used small samples. We report a preregistered replication with 240 participants who listened to self-selected and experimenter-selected excerpts while skin conductance and continuous self-report were recorded, with a subsample of 62 undergoing fMRI. Chills were reliably elicited by self-selected music but only sporadically by experimenter-selected music, and the association with nucleus accumbens activity was weaker than in the original reports. Anticipatory violation of harmonic expectation predicted chill onset more robustly than loudness change. We discuss implications for theories that treat chills as a unitary phenomenon.

title: Group singing versus receptive music therapy for depressive symptoms in older adults: a randomised controlled trial
abstract: Music therapy is widely used with older adults, but active and receptive approaches are rarely compared directly. In this three-arm randomised controlled trial, 186 community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over with mild to moderate depressive symptoms were assigned to twelve weeks of group singing, receptive music listening with a therapist, or a social activity control. Depressive symptoms decreased in all groups, with group singing showing the largest effect at week 12 and the only significant between-group difference at six-month follow-up. Adherence was highest in the singing arm. Improvements in perceived social connectedness statistically mediated roughly half of the treatment effect, suggesting that the social affordances of joint music making matter as much as the music itself.

title: Integrating Contextual Embeddings into Evaluation of Expressive MIDI Piano Performance
abstract: Objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performance typically relies on attribute-level statistics such as tempo deviation and dynamic range, which correlate only weakly with human judgements. We propose an evaluation framework that embeds performances together with their score context using a contrastively trained encoder, and measures the distance between a candidate performance and the distribution of human performances of the same score. Across three datasets covering 1,400 performances, our metric correlates with expert ratings at rho = 0.71, compared with 0.38 for the best attribute-based baseline. Ablations show that score context, rather than performance features alone, drives most of the improvement.

title: Metrical dissonance in West African timeline patterns: a corpus-analytic reassessment
abstract: Analyses of West African timeline patterns have long relied on a small canon of transcribed examples, often mediated through European notation. Drawing on a corpus of 640 field recordings from Ghana, Togo and Benin annotated by three analysts, we reassess claims about maximal evenness and rhythmic oddity. While the standard bell patterns do cluster near maximally even distributions, a substantial minority of regionally specific timelines do not, and their deviation is systematically associated with dance function rather than with ensemble size. We argue that the analytic emphasis on evenness has obscured a functional dimension of metrical organisation, and propose a revised typology grounded in performance context.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining Improves Low-Resource Automatic Music Transcription for Non-Western Instruments
abstract: Automatic music transcription systems are overwhelmingly trained and evaluated on Western piano recordings, and transfer poorly to instruments with different timbral and tuning characteristics. We investigate whether self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled recordings can close this gap. Using 4,000 hours of unlabelled audio spanning oud, guqin, sitar and kora, we pretrain a masked-spectrogram encoder and fine-tune on small annotated sets of 20 to 90 minutes per instrument. Note-level F1 improves by 9 to 17 points over supervised-only baselines, with the largest gains on instruments with pitch bending. Errors concentrate on ornamentation, which we analyse qualitatively with two performer-annotators.

title: What happens after the ensemble ends? A five-year longitudinal study of secondary school music participation
abstract: Claims about the long-term benefits of school music participation are common but rarely tested longitudinally beyond graduation. We followed 1,120 students from four regions for five years, from their final year of secondary school into early adulthood, combining annual surveys with 60 interviews. Continued musical participation after graduation was strongly predicted by informal peer music making during school years, and only weakly by formal ensemble achievement. Students whose school experience centred on graded examinations were more likely to stop playing entirely. We argue that curricula optimised for measurable attainment may inadvertently undermine the lifelong participation they claim to foster.

title: Infants track melodic contour before they track absolute pitch: evidence from a cross-linguistic habituation study
abstract: Whether infants encode melodies primarily in terms of contour or absolute pitch remains contested, and existing evidence comes almost entirely from infants raised in non-tonal language environments. We tested 216 six- and eleven-month-old infants growing up in Mandarin-speaking and Dutch-speaking households using a habituation paradigm with transposed and contour-violating melodies. At six months, infants in both groups dishabituated to contour violations but not to transpositions. At eleven months, Mandarin-exposed infants additionally showed sensitivity to exact interval changes. The results indicate an early contour-first bias that is subsequently modulated by the pitch structure of the ambient language.

title: Do Music Recommendation Systems Narrow Listening Diversity? A Six-Month Field Experiment
abstract: Concerns that algorithmic recommendation narrows musical taste are widespread but rest largely on observational data. We report a six-month field experiment on a mid-sized streaming platform in which 12,400 consenting users were randomly assigned to the production recommender, a diversity-regularised variant, or a chronological feed. Catalogue-level diversity of listening increased modestly under the regularised recommender without reducing engagement, while the chronological condition reduced both diversity and engagement. Effects were concentrated among users with initially narrow listening profiles. We discuss why observational estimates of filter-bubble effects may be biased and release an anonymised dataset of aggregate listening statistics.

title: Tuning drift in unaccompanied choral singing: a study of 32 amateur and professional choirs
abstract: Unaccompanied choirs commonly drift in pitch over the course of a piece, yet the causes remain debated. We recorded 32 choirs, half amateur and half professional, performing the same three Renaissance motets, and extracted section-wise fundamental frequency trajectories. Drift was overwhelmingly downward and averaged 41 cents over a three-minute motet in amateur ensembles versus 12 cents in professionals. Drift magnitude correlated with the density of imperfect consonances at phrase joints rather than with overall duration or tempo, supporting an interval-chaining account over a fatigue account. Rehearsal-room reverberation time had no measurable effect.

title: Platform vernaculars and the short-form remix: how fifteen-second edits reshape song structure
abstract: Short-form video platforms have made fifteen-second excerpts a primary mode of musical circulation, but their effect on how songs are written is poorly documented. Combining an analysis of 2,300 charting tracks released between 2015 and 2025 with 24 interviews with songwriters and producers, we trace a measurable shortening of intros, earlier arrival of the hook, and a rise in what informants call the 'pre-drop reset'. Producers describe designing songs to survive decontextualisation. We argue that these are not simply commercial concessions but the emergence of a platform vernacular with its own aesthetic logic.

title: Streaming Source Separation with Sub-50ms Latency for Live Ensemble Monitoring
abstract: Existing music source separation models achieve high quality offline but are unsuitable for live monitoring because of algorithmic latency and lookahead requirements. We present a causal separation architecture combining a low-latency filterbank with a recurrent bottleneck, achieving 47 ms algorithmic latency on commodity hardware. On a newly recorded multitrack dataset of 60 live ensemble performances, our model reaches within 1.3 dB SDR of a state-of-the-art offline baseline while running at 0.31 real-time factor on a single CPU core. A pilot deployment with a jazz quintet indicates that performers can use separated stems for personalised in-ear mixes without perceptible delay.

title: Focal dystonia in professional musicians: prevalence, career impact and treatment pathways in a national cohort
abstract: Musician's focal dystonia is career-threatening yet epidemiologically under-characterised. Using a national registry linked to occupational records, we identified 428 professional musicians diagnosed over a fifteen-year period and matched them to 1,712 controls. Point prevalence was 1.4% overall, with a strong male predominance among keyboard and plucked-string players that was not present among woodwind players. Median time from symptom onset to diagnosis was 2.7 years. Early referral to a specialist centre was associated with substantially higher rates of return to professional performance. The findings support targeted screening in conservatoire settings.

title: Recording, repatriation and refusal: negotiating archival access in a Sámi joik collection
abstract: Ethnomusicological archives increasingly pursue repatriation of historical recordings, but the ethics of access are rarely negotiated with descendant communities on their own terms. Drawing on three years of collaborative fieldwork with Sámi families whose relatives were recorded in the 1950s, this article documents a process in which repatriation was welcomed while public digitisation was refused. We analyse refusal not as an obstacle to scholarship but as a positive assertion of sovereignty over sonic heritage, and consider what archival infrastructures would look like if designed around graduated and revocable consent rather than open access by default.

title: Are Music Foundation Models Learning Music Theory? Probing Harmonic Representations
abstract: Large audio foundation models achieve strong performance on downstream music tasks, but it is unclear whether they encode music-theoretic structure or exploit surface statistics. We train linear and non-linear probes on the intermediate representations of four publicly available models to recover key, chord function, cadence type and modulation. Chord identity is highly decodable throughout the network, whereas functional labels such as cadence type are recoverable only in middle layers and degrade sharply for non-canonical repertoire. Probing accuracy on eighteenth-century chorales substantially exceeds that on jazz and popular corpora, suggesting the models encode a Western common-practice prior rather than general harmonic competence.

title: Wolf tones on the cello revisited: a coupled-oscillator model validated on eleven instruments
abstract: The wolf tone remains one of the most familiar defects of bowed string instruments, and is conventionally explained by coupling between a string mode and the body's main air or corpus resonance. We develop a coupled-oscillator model that additionally accounts for bow force dependence and tailpiece damping, and validate it against measurements on eleven cellos of differing construction. The model predicts both the pitch and the severity of the wolf within a semitone and 3 dB respectively in nine of eleven instruments. It further predicts the placement of a suppressor mass that minimises the wolf without dulling the instrument's response elsewhere, which we verify perceptually with six players.
venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

title: A newly identified autograph fragment of Clara Schumann's Op. 20 variations
abstract: A single-leaf autograph fragment recently surfaced in a private collection in Leipzig and is here identified as a discarded draft for Clara Schumann's Variations on a Theme by Robert Schumann, Op. 20. Paper studies, watermark evidence and handwriting analysis date the leaf to the winter of 1853. The fragment preserves an abandoned fourth variation in the tonic minor whose figuration is closely related to the finale of Robert Schumann's Bunte Blätter. The article presents a diplomatic transcription and argues that the excision reflects a deliberate narrowing of the work's motivic argument rather than a compositional impasse.

title: Cross-Cultural Evaluation of Text-to-Music Generation: A Benchmark Beyond English Prompts
abstract: Text-to-music systems are almost exclusively evaluated with English prompts describing Western genres, which both overstates their generality and obscures failure modes. We introduce a benchmark of 3,600 prompts in eight languages covering thirty musical traditions, paired with reference recordings and evaluation rubrics developed with tradition-specific expert panels. Five publicly available systems were evaluated by 240 raters. All systems degrade sharply outside Western popular idioms, frequently substituting stereotyped instrumentation. Notably, prompts translated into English do not recover performance, indicating that the deficit lies in the audio prior rather than in text understanding.

title: Groove ratings depend on drummer identity, not only on microtiming statistics
abstract: Research on groove has focused on microtiming deviations as the primary determinant of the pleasurable urge to move. We tested whether performer identity contributes beyond such statistics. Ninety-six listeners rated 240 drum excerpts, half of which were resynthesised to preserve microtiming and dynamics while replacing timbre, and half of which had microtiming transplanted between drummers. Groove ratings tracked drummer identity even when microtiming was equalised, and transplanted microtiming did not transfer groove ratings across drummers. Timbral factors, especially cymbal decay and ghost-note dynamics, accounted for a larger share of variance than microtiming magnitude.

title: Music listening during chemotherapy infusion: a stepped-wedge trial in three oncology day units
abstract: Music listening is often offered informally in oncology day units, but its effects have rarely been evaluated at service level. In a stepped-wedge cluster trial across three units and 574 patients, we introduced a structured music listening offer with curated playlists and staff training. Patient-reported anxiety during infusion decreased by a clinically meaningful margin, and use of as-needed anxiolytics fell by 19%. Effects were larger for first-cycle patients. Staff interviews highlighted that the structured offer reduced the burden of improvising support, though playlist curation required ongoing attention to avoid unintentionally distressing associations.

title: Score-Following for Historically Informed Performance: Handling Ornamentation and Flexible Tempo
abstract: Score-following systems assume a relatively literal realisation of the notated score, an assumption that breaks down in historically informed performance where ornamentation is improvised and tempo is highly flexible. We propose a hierarchical alignment model that treats ornaments as insertions drawn from a learned, style-conditioned distribution, and couples note-level alignment with a phrase-level tempo process. Evaluated on 90 recordings of Baroque repertoire with expert alignments, the model reduces alignment error by 44% relative to a standard hidden Markov baseline and remains stable through extended cadenzas where the baseline loses track entirely.

title: Teaching improvisation without a jazz canon: an action-research study in five primary classrooms
abstract: Improvisation is nominally central to many primary music curricula but is often taught through jazz-derived materials unfamiliar to both children and generalist teachers. Working with five classrooms over two terms, this action-research study developed and iteratively revised a sequence grounded in children's existing play repertoires and local soundscapes. Video analysis of 40 lessons shows a shift from teacher-led call and response toward sustained child-initiated exchange by the sixth session. Generalist teachers reported markedly increased confidence, and the strongest predictor of pupil participation was the teacher's willingness to improvise audibly and imperfectly alongside the class.

title: Twenty years of the laptop orchestra: an oral history of institutional sustainability
abstract: Laptop orchestras proliferated in universities from the mid-2000s, yet many have quietly dissolved. Drawing on 38 oral history interviews with founders, students and administrators across eleven ensembles, this article traces the conditions under which such groups persist. Sustainability depended less on technical infrastructure than on whether the ensemble was embedded in credit-bearing curricula and whether repertoire was documented in a form that survived personnel turnover. Ensembles built around a single charismatic founder rarely outlived that person's tenure. We propose practical documentation practices drawn from the ensembles that endured.

title: Singing Voice Deepfakes: Detection Generalisation Across Languages and Vocal Techniques
abstract: Detection of synthesised singing voice is more difficult than speech deepfake detection because legitimate singing already involves extreme pitch and timbre manipulation. We assemble a corpus of 46 hours of authentic and synthesised singing spanning six languages and eight vocal techniques including belt, falsetto and throat singing, and evaluate five detection architectures. All detectors degrade substantially on techniques absent from training, with throat singing producing the highest false-positive rate for authentic recordings. Fine-tuning on as little as ten minutes of in-technique audio recovers most of the gap, suggesting that deployment requires technique-aware calibration rather than a single universal detector.

title: Schema theory and the galant style: what corpus evidence does and does not support
abstract: Schema-theoretic accounts of the galant style have become the dominant pedagogical framework for eighteenth-century music, but the empirical basis for specific schema inventories is seldom examined. Using a corpus of 1,050 annotated movements, we test three claims: that schemata occur at predictable formal locations, that their surface realisations cluster into discrete types, and that schema vocabulary shifts systematically across the century. The first and third claims find clear support; the second does not, with realisations forming a continuum rather than discrete categories. We suggest the pedagogical inventory be understood as a set of prototypes rather than a taxonomy.

title: Synchronised drumming increases prosocial behaviour in children only when tempo is jointly negotiated
abstract: Joint music making is widely claimed to promote prosociality, but experimental manipulations usually impose an external tempo. In three experiments with 384 children aged six to nine, we compared drumming to a metronome, drumming to a partner's fixed tempo, and drumming in which the pair had to converge on a shared tempo without instruction. Subsequent helping and sharing behaviour increased only in the jointly negotiated condition, and the effect scaled with how much each child adjusted toward the partner. Mere temporal alignment was insufficient. The results suggest that mutual accommodation, rather than synchrony per se, drives the prosocial effect.

title: Efficient On-Device Instrument Recognition for Field Recording Archives
abstract: Large ethnographic audio archives are frequently undescribed at the level of instrumentation, which limits discovery. Cloud-based classification is often precluded by rights restrictions that prevent recordings leaving institutional premises. We present a compact instrument recognition model, 3.2M parameters, trained with knowledge distillation and quantised to run on commodity archival workstations without a GPU. On a held-out set of 12,000 field recordings covering 84 instrument classes, the model attains 0.79 macro F1, within 4 points of a 90M-parameter teacher while running 22 times faster. We describe deployment at two national archives and the annotation workflow it enabled.

title: Absolute pitch is not all-or-none: latent profile analysis in 1,890 musicians
abstract: Absolute pitch is usually treated as a categorical ability, an assumption that shapes both genetic and developmental research. We administered a standardised note-naming test to 1,890 musicians recruited across twelve countries and applied latent profile analysis to the resulting accuracy and reaction-time distributions. A four-profile solution fitted best, including a substantial intermediate group with high accuracy on white-key pitches and near-chance performance elsewhere. Age of onset of training predicted profile membership continuously rather than dichotomously. Treating absolute pitch as binary appears to discard systematic and theoretically informative variation.

title: Sound systems, sovereignty and the politics of bass in Kingston's public space
abstract: Jamaican sound system culture has long been analysed in terms of technology and genre, less often as a spatial politics. Based on eighteen months of fieldwork in Kingston, including participation in twenty-two street dances and interviews with operators, residents and municipal officials, this article examines how low-frequency sound constitutes and contests claims to public space. Noise regulation is shown to operate unevenly along lines of class and neighbourhood, while operators mobilise technical expertise about bass propagation as a form of civic argument. The article contributes to debates on sonic sovereignty by foregrounding infrastructure rather than genre.

title: Rehearsal Room Assistant: Multimodal Feedback for Amateur Ensembles Using Audio and Pose
abstract: Amateur ensembles rarely have access to a conductor or coach during self-organised rehearsal. We describe a system that combines multichannel audio analysis with lightweight pose estimation from a single camera to provide feedback on intonation, entry synchrony and bow or breath preparation. In a four-week deployment with nine amateur ensembles, groups using the system improved measured entry synchrony by 28% relative to a matched control, though intonation improvements were not significant. Interviews indicate participants valued objective evidence for disputes that previously stalled rehearsal, but resisted feedback framed as scoring.

title: Vocal load in music theatre performers across an eight-show week: an ambulatory monitoring study
abstract: Music theatre performers sustain unusually high vocal demands, yet objective load data are scarce. Twenty-eight performers in three long-running productions wore ambulatory vocal dosimeters across a full eight-show week. Cumulative phonation time exceeded published occupational thresholds on five of seven days, and vocal doses on two-show days were more than double those on single-show days without a corresponding increase in recovery time. Off-stage talking during the interval contributed a larger share of total dose than expected. The findings support scheduling interventions and targeted education about non-performance voice use.

title: Consent, credit and compensation: musicians' attitudes toward generative music systems
abstract: Debates about generative music systems often invoke musicians' interests without systematically consulting them. We surveyed 1,412 working musicians across nine countries and conducted 36 follow-up interviews. Attitudes were far from uniform: session and production musicians reported the most immediate economic threat, while composers for media were most concerned about attribution. A large majority supported opt-in training regimes, but respondents distinguished sharply between training on recordings and training on notated scores. Compensation preferences clustered around collective licensing rather than individual negotiation, echoing existing performing-rights infrastructure.
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency

title: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in Parkinson's disease gait: dose-response evidence from a multi-site study
abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation improves gait in Parkinson's disease, but optimal dosing is unclear and protocols vary widely between centres. Across four sites, 208 participants completed a randomised dose-finding study comparing 20, 40 and 60 minutes of weekly cued walking over ten weeks. Gait velocity and stride-length variability improved in all arms, with 40 minutes producing nearly all of the benefit seen at 60 minutes and significantly outperforming 20 minutes. Benefits attenuated within eight weeks of cessation in all arms. Musical preference matching was associated with adherence but not with the magnitude of gait change.
venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

title: A Reproducibility Study of Twelve Music Emotion Recognition Systems
abstract: Music emotion recognition results are frequently reported on incompatible splits and annotation schemes, making progress hard to assess. We re-implement twelve published systems from 2018 to 2025 and evaluate them under a unified protocol on four datasets with harmonised valence-arousal annotations. Reported and reproduced results differ by more than five points of R-squared for seven systems, and the ranking of methods changes substantially once annotator disagreement is modelled explicitly rather than averaged away. Simple spectral baselines remain competitive on cross-dataset transfer. We release the harmonised benchmark and all re-implementations.

title: Learning by ear in the age of the tutorial video: transmission of Irish traditional fiddle style online
abstract: Oral transmission in Irish traditional music has partially migrated to video platforms, raising questions about what is preserved and what is lost. Combining analysis of 400 tutorial videos with interviews and lessons observed both online and in person, this article examines how ornamentation and bowing style are conveyed without co-presence. Ornament placement transmits well through repeated slow-motion demonstration, while bow-arm weight and the negotiation of tune settings within a session prove resistant. Learners who used video exclusively developed recognisably distinct rhythmic profiles, which established players describe with a consistent vocabulary of critique.

title: Perceptual thresholds for spatial reverberation mismatch in immersive music reproduction
abstract: Immersive music reproduction increasingly combines recorded ambience with synthetic reverberation, but tolerances for mismatch between the two are poorly specified. In a listening experiment with 42 trained listeners and 12 musical excerpts, we varied the mismatch in early decay time, interaural cross-correlation and early reflection direction between recorded and synthetic components. Listeners were far more sensitive to direction mismatch than to decay-time mismatch, detecting 15-degree offsets reliably while tolerating decay differences of up to 25%. Sensitivity was greatest for sparse chamber textures and lowest for dense orchestral passages, suggesting content-adaptive tolerances for production practice.

title: Background music and reading comprehension: a multi-lab replication finds no reliable effect
abstract: The claim that background music impairs or improves reading comprehension has generated a large and inconsistent literature. Eleven laboratories in eight countries jointly preregistered and ran a common protocol with 2,340 participants, manipulating lyrical content, tempo and self-selection. Across all conditions the effect of background music on comprehension was indistinguishable from zero, with confidence intervals excluding effects previously reported as medium-sized. Self-reported distraction did vary substantially between conditions but was uncorrelated with performance. We discuss why subjective experience and objective performance may diverge in this domain.

title: Long-Context Modelling of Full-Length Recordings for Structure-Aware Music Retrieval
abstract: Most music retrieval systems operate on excerpts of thirty seconds or less, discarding the large-scale form that distinguishes many works. We investigate long-context encoders that ingest full recordings of up to twenty minutes using a hierarchy of learned summarisation tokens. On a retrieval benchmark of 24,000 classical and progressive rock recordings where distractors share local texture but differ in form, our model improves mean reciprocal rank by 31% over excerpt-averaged baselines. Attention analysis indicates the model attends preferentially to sectional boundaries, and performance degrades gracefully when recordings are truncated.

title: Reconstructing the sound of the eighteenth-century Venetian ospedali choir from payroll and architectural records
abstract: The all-female choirs of the Venetian ospedali are among the most discussed and least documented ensembles of the eighteenth century. Combining payroll records identifying voice types and seniority with architectural surveys and acoustic simulation of the surviving chapel galleries, this study reconstructs plausible ensemble sizes, seating and balance for the 1740s. The simulations indicate that the elevated and screened galleries produced substantially more diffuse sound at the congregation than has been assumed, which bears directly on debates about the audibility of contrapuntal detail in Vivaldi's sacred works written for these institutions.

title: Predictive processing accounts of musical pleasure: a critical review of the evidence
abstract: Predictive processing has become the dominant framework for explaining musical pleasure, typically via the interplay of expectation and its violation. This review evaluates the empirical support for three core commitments of the framework: that surprise is quantifiable from statistical models of the corpus, that pleasure follows an inverted-U function of surprise, and that precision weighting explains individual differences. Support for the first is strong, for the second mixed and highly dependent on stimulus range, and for the third largely indirect. We identify specific experimental designs that would discriminate between predictive processing and simpler familiarity-based accounts.

title: Book Review: The Cambridge Companion to Music and Migration
abstract: This volume assembles twenty-two essays on music and migration, ranging from medieval itinerant musicians to contemporary refugee music-making. The editors have assembled an impressive geographical range, though the balance tilts toward the twentieth century. Individual contributions are uniformly well researched, and the closing section on methodology will be valuable for graduate teaching. Some readers may wish for a more sustained engagement with economic history, which appears only intermittently.

title: Editorial: new directions for the journal's fiftieth volume
abstract: As the journal enters its fiftieth volume we take the opportunity to describe forthcoming changes to the editorial process, including a new registered reports track and revised guidance on data sharing. We also thank the outgoing associate editors for their service and welcome four new members of the editorial board.

title: Neural entrainment to musical beat predicts sight-reading fluency in conservatoire students
abstract: We report that EEG-measured neural entrainment at the beat frequency predicts sight-reading fluency in 88 conservatoire students, with entrainment strength accounting for 34% of variance after controlling for practice hours. The effect was specific to the beat frequency and did not extend to metrical subdivisions.

title: Timbre space of historical woodwind instruments: a preliminary dataset description
